title: Cadwal's Button and the Big Award
markdown:
Cadwal Butterfield’s rooftop workshop was his favourite place in the world. Clocks ticked in gentle agreement. Jasmine from the window boxes sweetened the oil-and-brass smell. Every gear had a home. Every winding key lay in a row, smallest to largest, as if they might be inspected by someone who understood what a row was for.

This year, someone would. The Tidy Tickers award was coming: a golden clock trophy for the tidiest, most precise clockmaker in town. Cadwal had polished every surface until it answered the light. He had oiled every spring until it sang.

He wanted that trophy the way a cat wants a sunbeam: completely, and with a little shame about how much.

A tremor sometimes ran through his whiskers all the same. What if everyone saw only the shine and missed the careful work beneath? What if they saw nothing at all? The thought made his heart give a small, unprofessional lurch.

Judging day arrived with air as still as a balanced pendulum. Mayor Mildred was due any moment. Her hats were as grand as her pronouncements. Cadwal’s tools stood like a quiet parade. The clocks chimed a harmonious greeting, which he had, if he was honest, rehearsed.

He smoothed his whiskers.

Then his paws wobbled.

The prize magnifying glass — the one that made the smallest springs look as big as teacups — was gone.

His carefully built calm came apart like a tangled string. His pads felt damp. The workshop, which had been a sanctuary of order, suddenly looked like a place where things could hide.

He had to find it.

He peered under benches. He looked behind grandfather clocks that ticked a little too loudly, as if time itself had opinions. A tin of pinions rattled when he knelt. A winding key rolled and stopped against his boot, pointing, unhelpfully, at nothing.

The jasmine, usually a pleasure, thickened until it felt like a velvet curtain. His heart thrummed like a runaway escapement.

A sparkle near the polishing cloth.

Joy, then not. He picked it up. A button. A very shiny brass button with tiny carvings, the sort of thing that wanted to be important and was not a magnifying glass.

Cadwal stared at it. The search had made a jumble of his morning. He had wanted the award so badly that the missing glass felt like a verdict. The button sat in his paw, cool and useless and oddly honest.

From the stairwell came the particular rustle of a mayor’s hat arriving on time.

Mayor Mildred cleared her throat in the doorway.

“Mr. Butterfield,” she said, and her voice was softer than her hat. “It appears you’ve lost your magnifying glass. And perhaps a little of your usual calm.”

Cadwal looked at the button. He breathed in jasmine and oil until the breath reached the bottom of his ribs.

“I did,” he said. The words wanted to be tidier. He let them be true instead. “I got so busy hunting one small thing that I forgot why I like this room. It isn’t only the shine.”

From the doorway, Edie peered in. She was a tall, gentle giraffe, and she had a way of making ceilings feel friendly.

“Cadwal,” she said, as if wind were speaking through grass. “The clocks still tell the time. The work is still here. Sometimes the important things are the ones we almost miss.”

Mayor Mildred’s smile went crinkly. She looked at the lined-up keys, the singing springs, the cat who had decided not to invent a tidier excuse.

“For an impeccable workshop,” she said, “and for not pretending this morning was perfect, I have a commendation. Exemplary Effort and Spirit.”

She set a small silver medal in his paw. It was not the golden clock. It felt, just then, like the right weight.

Later the sky went apricot and rose. Cadwal sat with Edie while the clocks kept their ordinary promises. She reached to a high shelf — the sort of shelf a giraffe considers convenient — and handed him the magnifying glass. It had been sitting there. He had left it there. Of course he had left it there.

A ladybug no bigger than his thumbnail landed on the rim. A tiny iridescent mark on its shell caught the last light, like a button that had learned to fly.

Cadwal did not flinch. He did not start another search. He watched the ladybug decide the glass was a perfectly good hill, and he let the workshop be tidy enough, and his, and finished for the day.
characters: Cadwal (an ambitious cat clock repairer), Edie (a giraffe friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
author: StoryGen Community
